words.etymon: unmapped in slab (proper noun not in word list); = univerbated *dyew- (voc. *dyéw) + *ph₂tḗr

cognate: Gk Ζεύς / Ved. dyáuḥ / Lat. Iou- (Iu-piter) < *dyḗws; Gk πατήρ / Ved. pitā́ / Lat. -piter (pater) < *ph₂tḗr. Every member of the pair is cognate in all three branches; Latin has univerbated the vocative phrase *dyéw ph₂ter into the theonym Iuppiter (Diespiter).
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek and Vedic; in Latin the phrase has been fused into a single name (univerbation), with pater still separately usable in prayer (Iane pater, CatAgr 134.3)
shared_syntax: theonym 'Sky' + appositive 'father' (nominative of designation, or vocative of address in prayer): πατὴρ ... Δία, dyauḥ pitā, Iupiter (vocative) in a sacrificial address
context: Religious designation of the sky-god as father. AVŚ 3.23.14 and 9.10.23 pair dyauḥ pitā with pṛthivī mātā ('Father Sky, Mother Earth'); AVŚ 9.10.23 repeats RV 1.164.33. Aristotle Pol. 1259b quotes the Homeric formula πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε for Zeus (so the prose carries a verse formula), and Homer has Ζεὺς πατήρ / Διὶ πατρί often. Cato Agr. 132 is a prayer at the daps offering addressing Iupiter dapalis in the vocative, the same speech act as Ved. dyaùḥ pítar (RV 6.51.5) and Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ. Not chance: a specific theonym + kin-term apposition, with fully regular cognates in three branches and fossilised as one word in Latin.

note: Slab is mostly Aristotle Problemata/Politica and Cato Agr. prose with automatic partners; one solid inherited formula (Dyaus pitar / Zeus pater / Iuppiter). Leads considered and not claimed: θνητοῖσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισιν (Theognis 804, B-e0345) ~ amartyo martyena (AVŚ 9.10.15, B-2ac4e) — merism only in context lines and the in-slab Greek words are renewals, not cognates; svédam āsiṣvidānā (RV 10.106.10) ~ ἱδρώτων/ἱδροῦμεν (B-59274) — no cognate-object figure in the slab Greek (Il. 4.27 ἱδρῶ ὃν ἵδρωσα is the real parallel but outside the slab); waking/sleeping (jāgrat/svapan ~ ὕπνος/ἐγρηγορέναι, B-ac011, B-a5d79) and winter/summer (hima/ghraṃsa ~ χειμών/θέρος) — generic contrasts with incongruent contexts.
